title: The Council of Four Lands
hookLine: Polish Jewry governed itself through an elected council

cards: The fair at Lublin is loud: wagons of grain and cloth, horses being traded, merchants shouting prices in several languages. Jewish traders are everywhere.
But in a room off the market, rabbis and community leaders from across the region sit around a table with ledgers and letters. They are not here to sell anything. They are here to govern.
Today, the name of that table.

teach.b: In the kingdom of Poland and Lithuania, Jews lived in their own communities, each called a kehillah, with its own leaders, courts and charities.
Above them, Polish Jewry built something larger: a council of regional leaders, chosen by their communities, who met regularly at the great fairs, where people traveled anyway.

In Hebrew it was the Va'ad Arba Aratzot, the Council of Four Lands, after the regions it spoke for. What did it do? The crown taxed the Jews as a group, and the council divided that bill among the communities.

It made rules for trade, schools, the printing of books, and ransoming captives, which mattered terribly after the hard years we heard about this week. And it spoke for Polish Jews before the king and his officials.

In the Torah, Moses tries to judge every case himself, from morning to evening, until his father-in-law Jethro warns he will wear himself out, and advises him to choose capable, trustworthy people to share the work.
Hillel, in the Mishnah, adds: don't separate yourself from the community.
Self-governing did not mean free of the king; the council worked inside a kingdom that could change the rules.
But for a long time, Polish Jews collected their own taxes, judged their own disputes and taught their own children, through people they had chosen.
In the end the Polish government dissolved the council, and the kehillot carried on without it.

how: Jewish communities today still run their own synagogues, schools, burial societies and charities through boards and committees chosen by their members.

games.why: the council divided the tax among the communities and spoke for Polish Jews before the king and his officials.

practice: Picture the groups you belong to, a street, a congregation, a school, a team, a family chat, and ask which one could use a little more of you.

Moses learned he couldn't carry it all, and someone may be carrying too much right now; let one concrete idea come, one hour or one job. If you pray, you can pray for that community in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Kehillah. A self-governing Jewish community in Poland and Lithuania, with its own leaders, courts and charities, joined by councils like the Council of Four Lands. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a council, an assembly that meets at an appointed time.

carryVoice: Your line: self-governing. A people can carry its own shared life, together. See you tomorrow.
